justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for the underlying asset across all three horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 148.5 was driven primarily by recent price momentum and the assumption of mean-reverting intraday behavior around the prevailing trend. At the one-week horizon, the slight uptick to 149.2 reflects a continuation of that trend with minimal expected catalysts to disrupt it, essentially extrapolating near-term drift while acknowledging that weekly closes tend to revert toward recent moving averages. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of 151.0 incorporates a modest growth premium consistent with the broader macro environment at the time, assuming no major regime change in monetary policy or risk sentiment.

The confidence interval widths expand meaningfully as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval of 145–152 is relatively tight because short-term price variance is anchored by liquidity and intraday mean reversion. By one week, the interval widens to 142–156 as the cumulative effect of news flow, positioning shifts, and macro data releases becomes harder to anticipate. At one month, the interval of 136–166 is quite wide because a full month introduces earnings cycles, central bank meetings, geopolitical developments, and sentiment shifts that are fundamentally unpredictable at the time of the forecast.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected hawkish policy surprise, a credit event in a systemically important institution, or a sharp deterioration in macroeconomic data could produce a sell-off well below 136 within a month. On the upside, a positive earnings surprise, a dovish pivot signal, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices above 166. The one-day interval is also vulnerable to gap risk from after-hours announcements or geopolitical shocks that bypass normal intraday price discovery entirely, meaning even the tightest interval carries tail risk that standard volatility models may understate.
